articles.title: Trump agent’s ‘dead to me’ rant exposes ‘compelling’ motive in shooting: ex-prosecutor
articles.description: A former federal prosecutor said newly surfaced emails from a Trump immigration agent point to a motive in a deadly shooting. Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney, said Wednesday on her Substack show "Civil Discourse with Joyce Vance" that emails in which ICE officer David Brouillette told his sister she was "dead to me" amount to "strong, compelling evidence of motive" in the July killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine. Vance was joined by New York Times reporter Katie Benner, who reported with a colleague Wednesday that Brouillette's sister shared 2021 emails in which he lashed out at her Colombian partner, a man living in the U.S. legally. Benner's reporting also found Brouillette was brought on during the Trump administration's rush to staff up deportation ranks, and that his background report was not fully reviewed before he was put in the field. ICE has denied lowering its hiring standards and declined to confirm Brouillette fired the shots. Benner read one of the emails on air, which Brouillette sent after his sister asked relatives to record birthday messages for her toddler. "Tell your partner he can take his non-citizen a— back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries," Brouillette wrote. "You're dead to me, Liz. Enjoy it. Dead to me." Vance, who said she handled civil rights prosecutions during 25 years at the Justice Department, explained that cases like this hinge on intent. "What you have to be able to do is to prove motive," Vance said. "These emails and the testimony of family members established that this was not someone who had the capacity to look at the man he ended up killing and view him as a human being." "The fact that there's such strong, compelling evidence of motive, I think, makes this ripe," she added. "It should be a federal prosecution." Benner said a lawyer for the victim's family was told that Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey, whose term ends Dec. 6, plans to release public findings before he leaves. Vance noted Maine has its own civil rights law mirroring the federal statute. "We sometimes forget that prosecutors are human beings just like everyone else, and they don't like to leave unfinished business behind when they go," Vance said. Benner also flagged Dec. 1, when Brouillette's probationary year ends and firing him gets much harder. "So I'm really curious to see whether or not he makes it through his one year," she said. articles.title: GOP lawmakers snipe at each other as their final legislative plans fall apart: report
articles.description: Senate Republicans can’t agree on whether to use their final weeks in power to pass a party-line Pentagon funding bill, Semafor reports. The party’s remaining tool is budget reconciliation, which lets a bill clear the Senate without Democratic votes. Many Republicans want to use it to give President Donald Trump money to rebuild weapons stockpiles drained by nine months of war with Iran. But senators told Semafor they have no plan yet. Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA) predicted a plan would emerge, but said that for now he wouldn’t recognize it “if it jumped up and yodeled and bit me in the butt.” Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-WI) said neither the White House nor leaders in either chamber have engaged with him, and that any push will have to come from rank-and-file members. Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD), who was reelected to his post this week, has repeatedly voiced doubt that the votes exist in either chamber. Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker (R-MS) and Sen. Jim Banks (R-IN) are pressing for a bill. Banks said it’s meant to supply the military, not fund the war. Sen. Rand Paul promised to vote no and said the bill would defy the election results. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) questioned why Republicans would pursue it. Meanwhile, Sens. Susan Collins (R-ME) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), two senators known for occasionally breaking with the party, have reservations about using reconciliation. Semafor reports many Republicans see the war as a leading cause of their midterm losses. It says frustration is also growing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who survived a House impeachment effort on Tuesday. Sen. John Hoeven (R-ND), who is close to Thune, said a party-line bill would give Republicans bargaining power with Democrats ahead of next month’s funding deadline. Other senators want to add provisions on living costs, elections and farm aid. Sen. Jim Justice (R-WV) said the party is trying to fit too many priorities into one bill, but that he may support it anyway. Reporter Burgess Everett notes the Senate has just four weeks of session left on its calendar, though Thune is open to adding time, and argues Republicans are already behind.

articles.title: Manhood review – a mind-boggling visit to the penis enlargement doctor who promises ‘better sex than ever’
articles.description: Can men mend their broken self-esteem with a thicker penis? This documentary about the patients of a Dallas clinic offering PhalloFill® treatment suggests there might be something deeper here In Bill Moore’s Dallas clinic, every man who drops his pants and lies on the treatment table, braced for the needle, has come looking for something without being sure what it is. As far as their physical selves are concerned, they know exactly what they want, and they are handing over thousands of bucks to pay for it: they all crave a thicker penis. Whether this will mend their broken self-esteem, though, is not clear. Daniel Lombroso’s documentary about Moore and his patients doesn’t know precisely what it wants either, as it floats between sad stories of modern male self-image that never merge into a singular takeaway argument. Is it about looksmaxxing and the manosphere? At least one participant has picked up questionable ideas from big, bad podcasts, so yes. But the film is also interested in pornography’s flooding of male brains with extreme imagery, and how unrealistic beauty goals for women can make insecure men blame their ills on their own imperfect appearances. It’s concerned with shame, trauma and homophobia too. Continue reading...

Red-state GOP gets sharp rebuke as top court kills their election scheme
articles.description: The Oklahoma Supreme Court on Tuesday struck down a 2025 state law that placed new limits on the initiative petition process, according to the Oklahoma Policy Institute. The court held that Senate Bill 1027 is “unconstitutional and void in its entirety” and can’t be enforced, the group said in a statement. The Legislature passed the measure in 2025. OK Policy says it would have made it harder for ordinary Oklahomans to put issues before voters as state questions, and that its own analysis found the law would have shut millions of registered voters out of the petition process. Opponents sued, arguing the law threatened a fundamental right in the state constitution and created needless barriers to citizen-led ballot measures. Cole Allen, an OK Policy analyst who has tracked the bill since its introduction, called the ruling a victory for Oklahomans’ constitutional rights. “Political power belongs to the people,” he said. He urged residents to stay alert for new attempts to restrict the petition process, and said lawmakers should respect the decision and not revive the issue. Allen said legislators’ time would be better spent on affordability and public schools. It's the latest setback to Republican efforts around the country to shut down the ballot initiative process in states that have one; many GOP-controlled states have seen voters passing policies at odds with the legislature, from Medicaid expansion to safeguarding abortion rights. Missouri Republicans faced their own blow in the midterm elections, as voters simultaneously overturned their mid-decade congressional gerrymander and passed new limits on the legislature's ability to pass bills nullifying citizen ballot initiatives.

articles.title: House Republicans block Hegseth impeachment effort as Democrats vow to try again
articles.description: The Republican-controlled U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday voted to effectively kill the articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — for now — by blocking their consideration on the House floor and sending them back to the Judiciary Committee, where GOP leaders can hold them up until the next Congress is seated in January 2027. Democrats — who voted unanimously Tuesday against shelving the impeachment effort — will have a large House majority next year after winning at least 255 seats in last week's midterm elections. They have already vowed to try to remove Hegseth from office when they take control of Congress. "In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker, said at a rally last month. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, reintroduced the articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, alleging that the embattled Pentagon chief had committed "high crimes and misdemeanors" and abused the power of his office by violating the War Powers Resolution, conducting military operations without congressional authorization and ordering unlawful military actions in several countries. On Tuesday, Massie was the only Republican who broke with his party and voted to keep the articles of impeachment alive. Before Tuesday's vote, Hegseth struck a defiant tone in a Pentagon news briefing. He described the impeachment efforts as "a farce" and insisted that "none of these are high crimes or misdemeanors — they are partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military." He added, "That's what it is. Policy disagreements. Not high crimes. Not misdemeanors. Not treason. Not bribery. Not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause." While Hegseth did not mention Massie by name, he criticized the actions of a "disgruntled congressman" and said the "proper remedy" for a policy disagreement was legislation. "It's a political spectacle," Hegseth said. "A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. Time for one man's final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president." He added, "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage." Hegseth also said the resolution suggested the U.S. would punish its own military for carrying out its job. "Let's be clear about what this resolution actually does," he said. "It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership." In response, President Trump posted on Truth Social that Hegseth had earned an "'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" for his defense against Massie. Trump described Hegseth as "perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country," adding, "Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!" The expected impeachment filing came as Congress returned to Washington, D.C., to begin a lame-duck session following the historic rout that the GOP suffered in last week's midterm elections. Hegseth has been facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran, which some top Republicans — including Trump — blame in part for the drubbing that cost them control of Congress. "Despite the absence of a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack upon the United States," Massie said in a speech on the House floor, "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation." Massie said Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law." His actions thus "warrant impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States," the Kentucky Republican said. Earlier, Trump told CNN at a White House press conference he would "stand by him," saying that he believes Massie "has a lot of hatred in his heart." Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the GOP primary — first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote. It's unclear whether Massie's impeachment effort would have succeeded on the House floor under Republican control. Massie had previously told ABC News he was "confident" there would have been "enough GOP defectors for it to pass." Trump has repeatedly insisted that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet. "No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters last week. The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor. "I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat. CBS News, however, reported last week that Trump "has been asking advisers" whether he should stay or go. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices. He has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, the Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 6, while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict. Trump acknowledged on Nov. 4 that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X. "The reason we lost is the war." The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did. Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning." "He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress." Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it." Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said on Nov. 6 that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth." "We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran," Comer told NewsNation. "No one's happy about Iran." When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list. Hegseth, for his part, has remained defiant. In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Nov. 5, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit. "A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/house-republicans-block-effort-to-impeach-hegseth-in-near-party-line-vote-231716935.html
